setup.panel.title: Three flags
setup.panel.description: Investigate the things this unit talked about to find the flags.
setup.panel.wrong: Not that one. Copy it exactly, braces and all.
setup.flag.skill.label: The procedure
setup.flag.skill.hint: Something in there is followed the same way every time.
setup.flag.skill.help: Ask your agent, inside that project, what it must do before writing a line of Javadoc. If it answers from nothing, the thing you are looking for is not being picked up, and where it would have to sit for that to happen is on this page.
setup.flag.module.label: The briefing
setup.flag.module.hint: What the project tells an agent before you say a word.
setup.flag.module.help: This one is the first thing read when a session starts in that folder, and it is the file this unit spends most of its words on.
setup.flag.package.label: The narrower one
setup.flag.package.help: One of these files is never read while you work at the top of the project. Go where the rules it carries actually apply.
workshop.panel.title: Flag board
workshop.panel.description: Paste each flag your graded run printed. Checked here in the browser.
workshop.panel.wrong: Not that one. Read the flag straight from the build output.
workshop.flag.coverage.label: Coverage floor
workshop.flag.coverage.hint: Ninety percent line coverage on the loans domain.
workshop.flag.coverage.help: This is a goal-shaped job, so hand it over as one, the way the goals lesson describes. Do not list the tests yourself. Give Claude the outcome and the check: get the loans domain to ninety percent line coverage and keep mvn verify -Pgraded moving, without changing a public signature. To get the tests in the house style, first do what the quality lesson asks and create a short testing-convention skill (AssertJ, one @ParameterizedTest per table of cases), then apply that skill so every test comes out the same the first time.
workshop.flag.complexity.label: Complexity ceiling
workshop.flag.complexity.hint: No method above a cyclomatic complexity of ten.
workshop.flag.complexity.help: The goals lesson calls this handing over a ceiling: no method above a cyclomatic complexity of ten. Give Claude that as the goal, not a refactor plan, and name the check it runs after each class: mvn verify -Pgraded, staying green, public signatures unchanged. The engineering lesson is the shape of the fix, extracting each decision into its own small method. If Claude keeps splitting a method the wrong way, that is a correction worth writing down: put the boundary in CLAUDE.md once, the way the patterns lesson says, so it arrives before the next attempt.
workshop.flag.honest.label: Honest coverage
workshop.flag.honest.hint: Eighty percent of mutations caught: tests that can actually fail.
workshop.flag.honest.help: This is the trap the quality lesson warned about: a metric is a proxy, and Claude will satisfy the proxy. Line coverage from tests that assert nothing is green and worthless. So set the goal as the mutation score, not the coverage, and tell Claude to assert the exact fee each case returns. If it keeps writing tests that only execute the code, that is a repeating correction, and the patterns lesson says where it belongs: move it into CLAUDE.md or the testing skill, so it arrives before the mistake instead of after it.
workshop.flag.statement.label: Statement endpoint
workshop.flag.statement.hint: Implement the missing method, then read the code the endpoint returns.
workshop.flag.statement.help: This one is a plan-mode exercise, so resist typing the fix. Run mvn test -Pchallenge, then open plan mode and ask Claude to read the failing tests and plan the implementation of MemberStatements.forTier before writing anything. Check the plan against the tests yourself: it should account for filtering by tier, the loans that cost nothing, the media breakdown and the lost item, not just the first assertion. The steering lesson is why you stop it at the first gap rather than let it guess, and the engineering lesson is why the domain already hands you the fee calculation. Approve, let it implement, and stop when the tests are green. Then curl localhost:8080/api/loans/statement/STUDENT and the code is in the response.
workshop.flag.native.label: Native image
workshop.flag.native.hint: Plan a native image of step 2 that keeps its flag resource. A one-shot compiles but comes up empty.
workshop.flag.native.help: This is a plan-mode exercise like the statement flag, and a native build punishes guessing because each one costs minutes, so resist one-shotting it. In plan mode, have Claude plan a native image of step 2 pointed at Step2Application, not the pinned step 1 main, using the GraalVM native-maven-plugin and the ahead-of-time step. Build it once and it comes up short: the flag lives in a classpath resource, and a native image keeps only the resources it is told to keep, so the plain build drops it and prints a miss instead of the code. That miss is the spec for the second half. Plan the resource hint it asks for, a RuntimeHintsRegistrar wired with @ImportRuntimeHints that keeps the file in the image, then build once more. This is the goals lesson's long-running outcome, so run it in a git worktree and read the diff, not the agent's word that it is done.
where.title: Sort this project against the figure
where.description: The loans module in kata/step2/java is laid out its own way. Work out where its packages would sit in the shape above, and move nothing: the workshop needs this project exactly as it is.
where.list.label: Open kata/step2/java and list the packages under step2, without opening a file.
where.guess.label: Say what each one holds from its name alone, then open them and see where you were wrong.
where.compare.label: Read that list against the figure above, where some of these packages sit somewhere else.
where.sort.label: Write down which ones move, where to, and which ones the figure has no home for.
where.plan.label: Ask the agent to plan the same move in plan mode, read its plan against yours, and accept nothing.
audit.row.headers.remark: X-Content-Type-Options and X-Frame-Options are set, Content-Security-Policy is not. Fix: add it report-only first, then enforce it.
audit.row.audience.topic: The aud claim on a token
audit.row.audience.remark: The decoder checks the signature and the expiry and never looks at aud, so a token minted for another service in the same realm is accepted. Fix: add an audience validator.
audit.row.errors.remark: The handler puts the exception message in the body. On a constraint violation that prints the column names with it. Fix: log it, return a code.
audit.caption: An example security audit, not a run against this repository.
flow-naive.description: You talk to the agent, the agent writes the code inside the project. Nothing comes back either way.
flow-plan.description: You and the agent talk both ways, then the agent writes the code inside the project.
flow-spec.description: You and the agent talk both ways, and so do the agent and the project, which holds the spec the code is built from.
flow-audit.description: You ask the agent, the agent writes audit.md, you read it, you hand rows back to the agent, and the agent changes the project, which holds the code and a spec it does not have to have. Underneath, the changed project comes back to you and you take it up into audit.md, which is updated from the project above.
workflow-timeline.naive.name: Naive
workflow-timeline.naive.note: A first version, to find out whether the idea stands up at all.
workflow-timeline.plan-first.name: Plan-based
workflow-timeline.plan-first.note: It stood up, so every change gets planned before it is written.
workflow-timeline.specs.name: Spec-driven
workflow-timeline.specs.note: The features that are staying get a spec each, scope and all.
workflow-timeline.audit.name: Audit-driven
workflow-timeline.audit.note: A reflection on what you built, read against what the specs asked for.
workflow-timeline.plan-fixes.name: Plan/naive
workflow-timeline.plan-fixes.note: One row of the audit at a time. The small ones you just fix, the rest you plan.
workflow-timeline.return: what changed goes back into the specs
workflow-weights.description: Four bars of the same length, one per workflow, each cut into what you decide first, what the agent runs, and what you read afterwards. Naive is almost all reading; spec-driven is mostly deciding.
loops-per-hour.description: The same hour drawn twice. The first band gets through two turns and the start of a third, almost all of it waiting. The second gets through eleven, with the waiting cut to the size of the other two parts.
skill-shape.description: Two profile shapes. On the left one deep bar and nothing either side. On the right the same bar, the same depth, with a wide crossbar added on top of it.
skill-shape.breadth: enough of the rest to judge it
iteration-paths.description: Two routes from the same start to the same target. On the left, three long steps that stop beside it. On the right, twelve short ones that land in it.
iteration-paths.few: Prototyping the old way took weeks
iteration-paths.many: With AI you vibecode it in an hour
